newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin reasserts authority, picks new minister.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin reasserts authority, picks new minister.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, reasserting his power after months of illness, named a liberal regional chief to a top cabinet post on Monday and the Kremlin said he was about to announce his planned government changes.

A presidential spokesman said Yeltsin had finally decided on the shape and line-up of the new government under a reshuffle which is being gradually unveiled. He would start publishing decrees formalising the changes later on Monday.

In a surprise move, Yeltsin offered Boris Nemtsov, the 37-year-old governor of the Nizhny Novgorod region, the chance to become one of only two first deputy prime ministers with former Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais.
"There is a very interesting variant," Yeltsin, confident, smiling and energetic, was shown on television as telling a slightly concerned-looking Nemtsov.

"Two young men -- you and Anatoly Chubais -- create a fresh young team in the government -- from scratch. No one (else) has been appointed yet. All candidates to the government would be agreed with the two first deputy premiers."
Yeltsin said Nemtsov had accepted the offer. His move appeared a decisive effort to end a stand-off blocking the announcement of the final reshuffle.
Russian liberals, who have criticised Yeltsin for a lack of progress in market reforms, hailed Nemtsov's appointment as a sign the president was committed to the reformist course.
"This is a movement in the right direction," RIA news agency quoted Viktor Sheinis of the liberal Yabloko party as saying.

Yeltsin, worried by the growing tension caused by chronic delays in wages and pensions and the government's inability to handle the crisis, has told Chernomyrdin to review the structure of the cabinet and dramatically improve its performance.
He has sent Chubais, his 41-year-old chief of staff with a reputation as a tough organiser, to reinforce the government.
Tass news agency said Chubais would be finance minister as well as a first deputy prime minister.
Yeltsin said that Nemtsov would handle social programmes, natural monopolies and deal with powerful regional authorities.
Political analysts said that by nominating Nemtsov Yeltsin also clearly meant to end the stalemate in bargaining between Chubais and Chernomyrdin over the cast of the new cabinet.
Yeltsin's initial idea was to leave Chernomyrdin, 58, with one powerful first deputy -- Chubais -- and let them form the government. But they have apparently failed to agree.
"There are at least two centres involved in the formation of the new government and trading is going on," independent member of parliament Alexander Pochinok told Interfax news agency.

The analysts have said that by putting in Nemtsov, who has good relations with both Chernomyrdin and Chubais, Yeltsin has built a bridge between them and also sent both a strong signal that he wants the reshuffle to go ahead promptly.

Interfering in the delicate issue of forming the cabinet, Yeltsin also reminded the other players that he held the top authority and that months of illness, caused by heart problems, were definitely over.

"I am in good form today. Today I am able, so to say, to rule the state and in fact in better form today than before the illness and I will of course rule Russia up to new elections in 2000," he said in an interview shown on Russian Television.

Political analysts say that Nemtsov's new job was crucial for the success of the cabinet. But they add that dealing with such sensitive issues could prove politically fatal for a man many have tipped as a strong presidential candidate for 2000.
Yeltsin broke the stalemate in the government reshuffle days before heading off to Helsinki for a summit with President Bill Clinton on Thursday and Friday.
U.S. and Russian officials have been trying to hammer out a deal that the two men could announce to ease tensions over NATO's expansion plans.

Yeltsin has laid out stiff terms for any softening of Moscow's objections to NATO's plans, saying on Sunday he would insist on a legally-binding treaty barring Western forces from being stationed in eastern Europe.
He made clear in the television interview on Monday that Russia's patience was not en dless.
"I don't want a return to the Cold War, I don't want it and our people don't want it, but for that there must be equal conditions in the world order," he said.
